1058.title: Holding history lightly
1058.hook: pride and grievance both can weigh down
1058.howItsDone: Muslim teachers point to Qur'an 2:134 and 49:13 when warning against boasting about ancestors or living in old grievances, and to the Prophet's forgiveness at the opening of Mecca as a model of setting old scores down.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aisha's answer, and your line: his character was the qur'an. Which habit did you try, the smile, the help at home, the sigh held back? Day one thousand fifty-eight.

Two backpacks. One is stuffed with trophies: the great libraries, the domes, the astronomers, the poets, the cities scholars crossed deserts to reach. The other is stuffed with stones: the sieges, the conquests, the colonial years, the old wrongs nobody ever answered for. This year has handed out both bags. Some people walk through life carrying only the first. Some carry only the second. And either one, carried long enough, bends the back. Today asks a quiet question. What do you do with a history that heavy?
screen: `A BAG OF TROPHIES.` → `A BAG OF STONES.` → `EITHER ONE BENDS THE BACK.`

segments.voice: First, a verse that can sound almost cold at first hearing. Speaking of the prophets and their families who came before, the Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "Those are a people who have passed away. Theirs is that which they earned, and yours is that which ye earn. And ye will not be asked of what they used to do." Some readers hear it as lifting a weight: nobody is credited with an earlier generation's glories, and nobody is charged with its sins. Each person's own account is the one that's open. Second, the trophies. The Qur'an cuts pride in ancestry down to size: "Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct." Not the best descended. Not the heir of the greatest empire. The best in conduct. By that measure, a golden age is something to learn from and give thanks for, not a badge anyone inherits. Third, the stones. Grievance can be just; real wrongs were done, and the Qur'an doesn't ask anyone to pretend otherwise. But the Qur'an also warns against letting old hatred bend present judgment. Pickthall again: "let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly. Deal justly, that is nearer to your duty." The wrong is remembered; it just doesn't get to write the next sentence. Fourth, a picture from the seerah. When the Prophet ﷺ entered Mecca, the city that had driven him out, the sources describe a general pardon for its people instead of a settling of scores. He knew that history from the inside. He carried it, and he set it down. Lightly does not mean forgetting. It means carrying history in your hands, where you can look at it, instead of on your back, where it bends you.
screen: `THEIRS IS THAT WHICH THEY EARNED.` · `THE NOBLEST: THE BEST IN CONDUCT.` · `LET NOT HATRED BEND YOUR JUSTICE.` · `MECCA: HE SET THE OLD SCORE DOWN.` · then, large: `YOURS IS THAT WHICH YE EARN.`

segments.voice: The practice: let one grievance go, or at least loosen your grip on it. Settle, and breathe out slowly. Find one old resentment, large or small: something done to you, to your family, to people like you. You don't have to decide it was fine. Just look at it, in your hands, not on your back. Breathe in, and name it. Breathe out, and let your hands open a little. If you pray, you can ask Allah for justice where it's owed and lightness for your own heart. If you don't, simply notice whether the weight shifts. The bell holds the time.
Holding history lightly. Theirs is what they earned, yours is what you earn: remembered, learned from, and not worn as a crown or a chain. Today's word.
Your line: carry it lightly. Today, when an old story about who wronged whom comes up, at home or online, add one sentence about what you can do now instead. Day one thousand fifty-eight.

1059.title: What will you leave?
1059.hook: a well, a book, a child's prayer
1059.howItsDone: Muslims give sadaqa jariya in forms such as funding wells, mosques, schools, copies of the Qur'an or trees, often on behalf of parents who have died, and children make du'a for their parents after prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two backpacks, trophies and stones, and your line: carry it lightly. Did one old grievance loosen, even a little? Day one thousand fifty-nine.

A well, dug in hot ground, still giving water long after the man who paid for it is gone. A book, copied and recopied, still being read by people who will never meet its author. A child, grown up now, raising her hands after the prayer and asking mercy for a parent who died years ago. Three things. None of them is a building with a name on it, or a fortune, or a title. And yet a saying of the Prophet ﷺ names exactly these three as the things that keep working after a life ends. Today, a question with no deadline except one.
screen: `A WELL, STILL GIVING WATER.` → `A BOOK, STILL BEING READ.` → `A CHILD, STILL PRAYING.`

segments.voice: First, the saying itself. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end except for three: a charity that keeps on flowing, knowledge that others benefit from, and a righteous child who prays for them. Three doors left open after the house is closed. Second, the flowing charity. Its Arabic name is sadaqa jariya, a charity that keeps on flowing. Abu Dawud keeps a story about a companion, Sa'd ibn Ubada, whose mother had died. He asked the Prophet which charity was best, and the answer was water. So Sa'd dug a well and said it was for his mother. A report in Tirmidhi also tells of a well in Medina that Uthman bought so people could draw from it freely. Water, given once, keeps giving. Third, the knowledge. This whole year has been full of it: scholars who wrote, teachers who taught a single student who taught another. A lesson passed on keeps working in someone else's life, whether or not anyone remembers who taught it first. Fourth, the child's prayer. The hadith's words are a righteous child who prays for the parent: a son or a daughter, after the prayer, asking mercy by name. Then notice what's missing from the list: wealth and power. A well can be a share in one. Knowledge can be one skill taught well. And the Qur'an widens the frame, in a verse that speaks of a record of what people sent ahead and the traces they left behind.
screen: `WHEN A PERSON DIES, THREE THINGS GO ON.` · `SADAQA JARIYA: CHARITY THAT RUNS LIKE WATER.` · `KNOWLEDGE THAT KEEPS ON WORKING.` · `A RIGHTEOUS CHILD WHO PRAYS FOR THEM.` · then, large: `WHAT THEY SENT AHEAD, AND THE TRACES THEY LEFT.`

segments.voice: The practice: plan one lasting good. Settle, and breathe. Look at the three doors. A well: is there something you could fund or join that keeps giving, water, a book for a library, a tree, a scholarship, a ramp? Knowledge: is there one thing you know that someone younger needs, a recipe, a skill, how to pray, how to fix a bike? A child's prayer: is there a child in your life you could be more present for? Choose one door. Then make it small enough to start this week. If you pray, you can ask Allah to accept it. If not, simply hold the plan. The bell holds the time.
What will you leave? A charity that keeps flowing, knowledge that keeps helping, a child who keeps praying: the three that go on. Today's word.
Your line: what will you leave? Today, take the first small step on the lasting good you chose: a message, a payment, a lesson offered, an hour set aside. Day one thousand fifty-nine.

screen: `DAY 1059 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CHAIN BACK TO HIM.`

1060.title: The chain back to him
1060.hook: every Muslim alive learned from someone, back to the companions
1060.tomorrow: Year three close: the long story
1060.howItsDone: Hadith are studied with their chains of narrators, and Qur'an recitation is traditionally learned face to face with a teacher; some receive an ijaza, a permission to teach that names the teachers before them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a well, a book and a child's prayer, and your line: what will you leave? Did you take the first small step on your lasting good? Day one thousand sixty.

Who taught you to tie your shoes? The name may be gone already. Try another one. Who taught you the first prayer you knew, or the first verse, or the first words of a language you love? Sometimes a name comes back for that one. Now ask who taught them. And who taught that person. For the Qur'an and the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ, Muslims say the thread doesn't vanish into fog. It runs back, teacher before teacher, to the companions who heard him. Each person along it is one link. Today, the chain.
screen: `WHO TAUGHT YOU?` → `AND WHO TAUGHT THEM?` → `BACK TO THE COMPANIONS.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Open a hadith collection and the reports begin with names: so-and-so told us that so-and-so told him, that so-and-so heard the Prophet say. That list of names is called the isnad, the chain a saying leans on. Scholars weighed each link: was this person honest, careful, did they actually meet the one they quote? Second, why it mattered. In the introduction to Sahih Muslim, the scholar Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak is quoted saying, in effect, that the isnad is part of the religion, and without it anyone could say whatever they liked. The chain was a guard against invention. Third, the chain is people, not paper. Qur'an recitation is still taught face to face, the student reading to a teacher who listens and corrects, and some receive a written permission, an ijaza, that lists their teachers, and their teachers' teachers. A student holding one is holding a list of names. Fourth, how the chain grows. The Prophet said, in Sahih al-Bukhari: convey from me, even a single verse. And in another hadith there: the best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it. So learning is only half of it. The isnad itself names particular transmitters, weighed one by one. But the command to convey asks for as little as one verse, and the same habit of passing on runs through lives no chain records. A mother teaching a du'a. A neighbor showing a new Muslim how to make wudu. A teacher who stayed late. Everything this year has told was carried this way. Not by a book alone, but by a chain of people.
screen: `ISNAD: SO-AND-SO TOLD US THAT…` · `A GUARD AGAINST INVENTION.` · `IJAZA: A LIST OF TEACHERS IN YOUR HAND.` · `CONVEY FROM ME, EVEN ONE VERSE.` · then, large: `LEARN THE QUR'AN AND TEACH IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank your teacher. Settle, and breathe. This time, start from the thing, not the person. Pick one thing you know by heart: a verse, a du'a, a recipe, a rule for fixing things, a line of advice. Say it to yourself once, slowly. Now ask where it came from. Whose voice did you first hear it in? That person is your link. Then try one step further back: where did they get it? If you don't know, that's a question you could ask them. Before the bell, shape one plain sentence you could send them: you taught me this, and I still use it. If you pray, you can make du'a for that teacher, living or gone. The bell holds the time.
The chain back to him. Isnad: teacher before teacher, link by link, back to the companions and the Prophet. Today's word.
screen: `THE CHAIN BACK TO HIM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a chain of people. Today, send your teacher the sentence you shaped, by message, by call, or, if they're gone, in a prayer. Day one thousand sixty.

screen: `DAY 1060 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YEAR THREE CLOSE: THE LONG STORY.`

1061.title: Year three close: the long story
1061.hook: from the cave of Hira to your nearest mosque, fourteen centuries of people
1061.carry: you are in the story now
1061.howItsDone: Muslims often make du'a for those who came before them in faith, using words like Qur'an 59:10, and many keep alive the names of the Prophet's companions and the scholars who followed by reading their lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the isnad, and your line: a chain of people. Did you thank the teacher you thought of? Today, the last day of year three. Day one thousand sixty-one.

Read. Tradition says that word came to a man alone in the dark, in a cave on a mountain above Mecca, and would not let him go. Now, a long way from there, a mosque on an ordinary street near you. Shoes in a rack by the door. A child running between the rows before the prayer starts. An older man folding a prayer mat. Between that cave and this doorway lie century after century of people, and this year has tried to meet as many of them as it could. Today, before a new year opens, we look back down the road.
screen: `A CAVE ABOVE MECCA: READ.` → `A MOSQUE ON YOUR STREET.` → `CENTURY AFTER CENTURY OF PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: On the first day of this year, your line was: people carried it. Here is who carried it. First, the Prophet ﷺ himself, in full this time. Mecca before the revelation. The orphan, the trader, Khadijah's husband. The cave, and the command that came there, in Pickthall's translation: "Read: In the name of thy Lord who createth." The years of persecution, the sorrow, Ta'if, the night journey, the road to Yathrib, and Medina. Second, those who walked beside him. The first circle. The mothers of the believers. His family. Early believers and later ones, the freed slave who called the prayer, the women who asked hard questions. Third, the hard chapter. The succession, the caliphs, the first split, and Karbala, told with Sunni and Shia memory side by side, neither one ranked. Fourth, the long road after. Damascus and Baghdad, al-Andalus and Cairo, Timbuktu and Samarkand, Istanbul, Isfahan, Delhi, Java, China. Scholars, poets, builders, rulers who were merciful and rulers who failed. The modern centuries. The houses of prayer. The holy days, kept across all of it. And these last days drew the lessons: unity builds, knowledge as worship, ordinary hands, mercy remembered, failures admitted, women who were there, many faces, the prayer that went on, back to the source, his character, history held lightly, what you'll leave, and the chain. That chain doesn't stop at the past. It runs through every person who learned something from the people in this year and passed it on. Whatever brought you here, faith, curiosity, a partner, a parent, you have now heard the long story, and in the loose sense of yesterday's chain, whoever hears a story and passes some of it on becomes part of it.
screen: `FIRST: THE PROPHET, IN FULL.` · `THOSE WHO WALKED BESIDE HIM.` · `THE SPLIT, TOLD WITHOUT RANKING.` · `THE LONG ROAD, CITY BY CITY.` · then, large: `READ: IN THE NAME OF THY LORD WHO CREATETH.`

segments.voice: The practice: remember all of them. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring back a few faces from this year, one at a time: Khadijah, Bilal, Fatima, Husayn, a scholar in Baghdad, a woman who founded a school, a grandmother you'll never know by name. In the Qur'an, those who came later are described praying for those before them. Pickthall's translation gives their words: "Our Lord! Forgive us and our brethren who were before us in the faith." If you pray, you can say that line for all of them. If not, simply hold the long line of people in your mind until the year closes. The bell holds the time.
Year three close. The Prophet in full, the companions, the caliphs and the split, and the long story of the people after. Today's word.
Your line: you are in the story now. Today, write down one name from this year you want to carry into the next, and why. Tomorrow, year four asks how and why. Day one thousand sixty-one.
